Witness: Dr. Elara Vantage, a seasoned engineer with extensive experience in power system analysis, observes the intricate dance of electrical currents swirling through a network of interconnected systems. In her mind, she sees a landscape of alternating voltages, each like a heartbeat, pulsating with power and complexity.

She reflects on the modern marvels of contemporary engineering, like the seamless integration of solar panels into the national grid, a testament to human ingenuity. These new additions to the power system have brought forth peculiarities, challenges that challenge the conventional wisdom.

Dr. Vantage thinks back to the day when the first solar panel was installed. It was a momentous occasion, but also a harbinger of change. Solar arrays, unlike traditional power sources, generate electricity that can flow in reverse, a phenomenon that disrupts the expected order of power distribution. This unusual behavior of power flow is what this research delves into, a topic that has gained urgency with the proliferation of distributed generation.

The paper introduces a sophisticated model, a labyrinthine equation set that captures the essence of this inverse flow. Constraints, like the cap on voltage and power levels, act as invisible walls, ensuring the system doesn't collapse under the pressure of chaos. Dr. Vantage visualizes these constraints as protective veils, safeguarding the delicate balance of power distribution.

This model isn’t just a theoretical construct; it’s a beacon of hope for a future where power systems are not only stable but also smarter, more efficient, and better prepared for the unpredictable. Optimization algorithms serve as the compass, guiding the system towards optimal solutions. With this tool in hand, engineers can navigate the complexities of power flow, turning the theoretical into practical application.

Case studies pepper the narrative, presenting the tangible impacts of this research. Each scenario paints a vivid picture, from the subtle adjustments made in local substations to the monumental shifts in national energy policies. These stories underscore the real-world implications, showing how understanding and managing inverse power flow can lead to a future where energy distribution is not just reliable but also anticipatory.

But it’s not just about solving problems; it’s about envisioning a future where technology meets humanity. Smart grids, born from this research, promise a world where energy isn’t just delivered but is also intelligently managed. The landscape of power distribution will transform, reflecting a society that values both efficiency and sustainability.

In Dr. Vantage’s mind, this isn’t just a scientific pursuit; it’s a journey of discovery. A quest to unravel the mysteries of the electrical universe, to harness its power for the greater good. With every step forward, the lines blur between science and magic, between the realm of theory and the reality of everyday life.

Under the vast, swirling clouds of secrecy, Georgia's government is unveiling a plan that feels like a breath of fresh air, or perhaps, just another breath of smoke. It’s called the hidden asset pardon, a measure to clear the underbrush of undisclosed wealth. As I, Witness X, watch this unfold, it's like tracking a ghostly trail, a series of whispers and vague hints that seem to lead nowhere until they suddenly converge into a solid path.

The announcement says that under this new scheme, individuals can lay down their concealed treasure without fear of criminal charges, just a hefty fine. The fine? It’s based on the value of the treasure—more the treasure, the steeper the fine. It’s estimated that in secret coffers and vaults, there lie billions of dollars—billions!

But here’s the catch, it’s not just any fines; it’s a balancing act. Higher the treasure, higher the cost to confess. The government aims to boost tax revenue and reduce corruption, but critics see it as a soft touch. "Leniency" they call it, a word that feels hollow against the clashing rocks of reality. But the supporters paint it differently, as a smart strategy, a way to nudge people out of hiding.

The plan? A massive campaign to inform and educate the populace, making them aware of the opportunity. A dedicated unit within the tax authorities will handle it, ensuring fairness and equality. It’s a delicate dance, trying to convince the masses that honesty pays off, or at least, a fine pays off.

It feels like a step towards clearing the air, but it’s still just a whisper in the stormy landscape of corruption. Will it work? Only time will tell, but for now, it’s a glimmer of hope amidst the shadows. And I, Witness X, watch, hoping for the best.

In the foggy dawn, the world seems a whisper away, and I'm here, standing in my kitchen, a witness to this ritual of preparing something extraordinary. The morning starts with 8 and a half cups of water, just a bit more than what I'd normally need, but these are no ordinary ingredients. I've got 4 small, crisp carrots, their vibrant orange skin still warm from the cold, and a few slices of celery, diced like tiny soldiers, ready to join the fray. A handful of cloves of garlic, minced with care, is a small explosion of flavor, and the white parts of my leeks, sliced into neat little squares, are like translucent onions, soft and mild, adding a touch of sweetness. 

These vegetables, along with the 6 fresh baby spinach leaves, are the base of this soup. Then there's that big, juicy turkey, its flesh cooked and then chopped or shredded into bits, almost tender like velvet now. A whole batch of tomatos, maybe equivalent to a bag of frozen tomatoes, are added next, their skins still attached and slightly rough to the touch, like tiny hands reaching out. There's also dried rosemary and two bay leaves, their aromas mingling, a bouquet of flavors that's been distilled from the market. And finally, a sprinkle of salt and pepper, the essential seasoning that brings everything together. 

In my mind, I picture the farmer who planted these vegetables, his hands moving like a skilled chef, and the butcher who cut that turkey, every slice as delicate as a feather. Each ingredient, from the crispy carrot to the tender tomato, carries a story, a memory, a connection to the earth and the hands that nurtured them. 

Now, onto the cornmeal dough. I mix 1 cup of cornmeal with 4 cups of hot water in my food processor, the grains clumping and the liquid blending into a dough, sticky and doughy. As I set it aside, I can almost feel the warmth of the stove, the steam rising, and the smell of fresh bread. I dust the countertop with a fine layer of potato starch, and roll out the dough, thin and fragile, like a piece of glass. It’s a dance, a choreography of the kitchen, and I’m the silent observer, the eye in the corner, watching the process unfold before me. 

The broth, simmering in the pot, is a symphony of vegetables, garlic, and the gentle sway of bay leaves. It’s a melody that sings, a symphony that fills the air, and soon it will be the canvas upon which all these elements will blend. The broth, rich and flavorful, is the heart of this soup, the soul that binds everything together. 

And then, the cornmeal noodles, each strand a tiny ribbon of hope, a promise that this dish will not only feed but also comfort. They’re rolled into strips, like a miniature version of lasagna, and they’re set aside, waiting for their moment to shine. I see them as tendrils, reaching out, stretching, and connecting with each other, forming a web of sustenance, a network that will carry the flavors through the broth. 

As I prepare the vegetables, I’m surrounded by the memory of the farmer and the butcher, their work imprinted on every ingredient, their care and attention a testament to the simple pleasures of life. This soup is more than just food; it’s a story, a history, a tribute to the people and places that have shaped me. It’s a reminder that even in the most mundane tasks, there’s beauty, depth, and meaning. 

Finally, the soup is complete, a harmonious blend of flavors, textures, and memories. It sits in front of me, a testament to the power of the kitchen, a celebration of the journey from seed to plate, a reminder of the connections that bind us all. And I am the witness, the silent observer, the keeper of this secret, this sacred ritual, and the essence of it all.

So, here we stand, in the shadow of a legacy, a chain of viscounts, a lineage of vision, a tapestry woven with the threads of history, a story told in the whispers of the past, a tale that continues, a legacy that lives, a legacy that lives in the eyes of the witness, Dr. Elspeth Grey, a witness to the passage, a witness to the story, a story of the Oxfuird viscounts, a story of the Maitlands, a story of the Maitlands, a story of the Maitlands, a story of the Maitlands, a story of the Maitlands.

In the vast, swirling ocean of academic research, I've been floating through the currents of a study about Nature Genetics, its peculiarities, and its selective ways. It's not just any study; it's a meticulous voyage into the waters of selective publication. They're defining the frequency of abstracts appearing in Nature Genetics articles using a logistic regression model. Are journals like Nature Genetics, each a unique island, publishing their own kind of fish? I can't help but think of them as islands, each with its own species of papers. As they sift through data, analyzing frequencies by author, journal issue, and journal field, they find something intriguing – there’s a significant association, but no significant difference between journal numbers (JSS). Like pebbles scattered on the shore, each paper seems to hold its place, even if the beach isn’t perfectly uniform.

They're comparing publications by geographic location and geographical journal issue type. Journals that are only journals, and those at the top of a field of specialization. The patterns are fascinating, almost like a dance, where each step tells a story. But the real gem here is the hypothesis they propose: that journals might publish only the best, ensuring that only the top-tier papers get a spotlight. It’s like they’re saying, “We select our fish, and we show them off.” It's a theory that makes sense, especially when you see how some manuscripts don’t get an abstract, while others do. Like a game of hide and seek, only certain stories get told.

In the first part, they use a logistic regression model, like a compass guiding the way. With these parameters, they formulate two hypotheses. The first is that journals publish papers of the same quality in the same field, much like how we expect consistency in a good fishing spot. The second is that they only publish papers that are either without competitors or have very few original articles. It’s a bit like the old adage that says, "No fish means no competition."

In the second part, they dive deeper. It's all about authors, issues, and regions. It's not just the manuscripts, but who wrote them, where they came from, and what they're doing. And the results are telling. Manuscripts by top journals get their spotlight, whether they have abstracts or not. They control for the fish’s status, how many friends it has, and its home, making sure everything’s equal before they cast their judgment.

All this happens within the context of a conference scheduled for the week of October 13, 2014. It's a whirlwind of ideas, theories, and hypotheses, each one more intriguing than the last. The study is a snapshot of the world of scientific publication, where every paper is a fish, and every decision made ensures that the best ones get their time in the limelight.

In this modernist stream-of-consciousness narrative, the witness, Charles, sees everything through Stevens' eyes, a butler at Darlington Hall. It's the 1930s, and Stevens is nearing his sixtieth year, having served Lord Darlington for over thirty years. Each step is a reflection of his devotion; he cherishes his profession, seeing it as more than just serving a master. His days are filled with meticulous routines, from preparing tea to attending to Lord Darlington’s needs. But beyond his duties, there's an emptiness; his connections outside of work are minimal, and the company he keeps is his father, another butler at a neighboring estate. 

As he watches his father grow frail, Stevens feels the weight of his own impending death. He realizes the choices he's made, the decisions that have defined his life. With each passing day, Lord Darlington's influence grows stronger, his ties to the Nazis becoming clear. The world around him shifts like waves, the air thick with tension. Stevens feels caught between his unwavering commitment to his master and his growing unease with his actions. 

Lord Darlington’s wealth and influence are both a beacon of power and a shadow of moral ambiguity. Stevens is torn, feeling the pull of duty and loyalty to his master, and the call to question his own beliefs. Each decision he makes, whether small or significant, becomes a battle within himself. He wonders if he can continue to serve someone whose views he finds abhorrent. 

Lord Darlington's world is shifting, and Stevens sees the changes like a kaleidoscope. In this ever-changing landscape, he must navigate his role as a butler and his relationship with his master. His reflections are constant, a tapestry woven with the threads of his past, present, and future. Stevens knows he can't change the world, but he can make his mark. His choices, his actions, will define his legacy. 

In the end, Stevens faces the remnants of his day and the legacy he hopes to leave. Each moment, each decision, is a piece of his story, a puzzle waiting to be solved. His journey is one of identity, loyalty, and morality, a quest to understand his place in the tumultuous 1930s.

In a café where the air is thick with the aroma of freshly brewed coffee and the soft hum of conversation, I'm sitting at a small wooden table, a cup of tea perched beside me. My eyes drift across the room, noting the faces of the people who pass by, their fleeting expressions and the way each sip of their drink reveals a story untold. There’s a man with his head buried in a newspaper, his fingers tapping against the page, and a woman with her gaze locked on the menu, her fingers tracing the edges as if she were feeling its texture.

I remember the day I made these Zeppoles. It was a Saturday morning, just like today, with the sun peeking through the blinds, casting a warm glow over the kitchen. As I whipped up the batter, the kitchen felt alive, like it was breathing alongside me. The ingredients blended together, melding into a smooth, creamy consistency, something out of a dream, a testament to the magic of a well-made dough.

The smell starts wafting through the house, the sweet, sugary tang filling my nostrils. I dip my finger into the bowl, the texture of the dough in my hand, cold and slightly sticky. It’s unlike anything else, like a piece of art, a tangible form of magic. I imagine the texture of the inside, the chewiness, the moisture, the airy solidity, like dense, moist cotton candy. And then, I think about the tops—cinnamon, chocolate, buttercream, the myriad possibilities that await, ready to be topped with a sprinkle of joy.

I’ve been making these Zeppoles for years, sometimes tweaking the recipe a bit, but always with the same goal in mind. When I first discovered them, they were the centerpiece of a meal, a way to end the day on a high note. Now, they stand alone, a treat to be savored, not just eaten. They’re not just Zeppoles; they’re a ritual, a moment to pause and savor the simple pleasures of life.

But the question remains—why are they worthy of a place on a website? Why should they be shared? Because they're more than just a treat; they're a memory, a story wrapped in a dough. They take a few minutes to whip up, a few minutes to bake, but they fill more than just the empty space on a plate—they fill the void in someone's heart, the gap in the moment when everything seems perfect.

I’ve made this recipe countless times, sometimes with a tweak here, a tweak there, but I think I’ve found the perfect balance now. These Zeppoles are not just about the dough and the filling; they’re about the moments, the stories, and the people who share them. And if I’m lucky, they’ll share them with others, passing along the secret ingredient of their own lives.

As I dip a Zeppole in the cinnamon sugar, the syrup melting onto the dough, I close my eyes, letting the flavors swirl around my tongue, tasting the memories, the stories, the secrets. This is a celebration, not just of food, but of life, the way it’s lived, the way it’s shared. In the quiet of a café, surrounded by strangers and acquaintances, I feel the weight of the world shift, a tiny act of kindness that might change someone’s day. These Zeppoles are not just Zeppoles; they’re the canvas on which we paint our lives.

Witness: Mr. Jameson, you see, I’ve been spending countless hours in front of the computer screen, absorbing the very essence of tranquility through Bob Ross’s videos. His voice, oh, it’s so soothing, a balm to the soul, making my mind drift away into these serene landscapes he creates. The way he talks, almost as if he’s having a heart-to-heart with the viewer, it’s so... comforting. His art, though, I must admit, is captivating. It’s like watching a masterclass in creating beauty, and it’s so easy to follow along, which makes it even more delightful. But, you know, there's this little niggle that keeps me on edge. His paintings do have a certain familiarity, a homogeneity, to them. It’s not that I don’t like it; I adore his signature style, those happy little trees, the fluffy clouds, it’s just that... well, I suppose it’s like when you drink the same flavor of juice day after day; it’s fine, but it starts to lose its charm. Still, let me tell you, that sense of calm, that feeling of being taken on a journey through these lush forests and serene oceans, it’s just... magical. This isn't a complaint about the joy and relaxation I derive from it, but a suggestion, a wish, that perhaps he might consider branching out, experimenting with different subjects or styles to keep things interesting. That said, I still find myself mesmerized by his creations, and the world of Bob Ross painting feels like a sanctuary to me.

The Lobster. Absurd, isn’t it? This film, The Lobster. Just watch it. Dystopian future, man. Single people gotta find someone, or else they become whatever they choose. It’s not just a movie; it’s a commentary. And I’m the witness. Watching David, Colin Farrell, alone in this strange hotel. Struggling, crying, trying. A desperate man, right there in front of me. 

The hotel, so surreal. An endless maze of mirrors, doors, and oddities. Each one a different story, a different person. These singletons, they’re so...quirky. One old lady in her underwear, another with a giant hat. They’re all vying for something, but what? Love, acceptance. Maybe even a chance to be normal. I don’t know them, but they’re all searching. So real, so vivid, and so twisted.

It’s not just the setting that makes it unsettling. The way they live, breathe, and move. Every ritual, every encounter, feels like a test. A trial, maybe, to see who gets picked. To decide who’s worthy. The pacing, slow and deliberate. Like time itself is slowing down, giving everything too much space. Atmosphere, thick and cold, the color palette muted, shadows everywhere. It’s like a ghost town, except these people are alive, breathing. And I can feel their desperation.

Then there’s the soundtrack, a symphony of discomfort. Unsettling sounds, dissonant notes, they play with my mind. Making me tense, making me squirm. All of it, the visuals, the sound, the performances. It’s raw, it’s real. It hits me hard. And David, he’s in there, fighting. Heartbreak, confusion, and I’m watching him. Watching him struggle, watching him find his way. It’s intense, it’s raw. It’s not easy to watch, but it’s worth it.

Colin Farrell, oh God, he’s doing it. He’s showing us this man’s desperation, his pain, his fight. It’s visceral, it’s real. His performance is nothing short of brilliant. It’s heartbreaking, it’s uncomfortable, but it’s real. And it’s so much more than just a movie. It’s a reflection, a mirror held up to society, to love, to life. It’s asking questions, making you question yourself. It’s not just a film, it’s a piece of art, a piece of the soul. It leaves you thinking, it leaves you feeling. It’s powerful, it’s profound. It’s The Lobster.

In this paper, we propose a technique, a topological image segmentation, for recognizing sign language. In my notes, I see that we start with the watershed transformation, using it to get the topological derivative from the gradient magnitude of the video frames. But you know, the gradient magnitude isn’t quite right; it needs some filtering. We need an isotropic filter to make things smoother, right? That isotropic filter stops the gradient from being swayed by just a couple of directions, making the watershed-based segmentation more reliable. 

Now, after applying this isotropic filter, we get segmented regions. Each region’s stats, its RGB histogram, get extracted, and we normalize it all. This gives us a bunch of features, but some are more important than others, so we select those using the Fisher score. It’s like choosing the best ingredients for a recipe, making sure we don’t waste any. 

Then, we feed these selected features into the k-NN classifier. It’s like having a brain that learns patterns, identifying the sequences of gestures in sign language. We’ve used this method on the Texas Instrument DLP Sign Language Gesture Database, and it’s performed pretty well, achieving a recognition rate of 95.6%. It’s like a perfect score in a game where every move counts.

In the heart of an ancient, forgotten land, whispers of a lost city stir in my mind. Lost in time and legend, a city where treasures lay beyond imagination, and secrets of ages past awaited discovery. Centuries passed, and still, no one found it, just crumbling walls and rusted metal. But then, a map appeared, a beacon of hope for the lost city’s secrets, guiding a young archaeologist named Sarah on a journey across treacherous terrain. Her team follows, determined, hoping to find the mythical streets.

Sarah sets out with a small team, her heart pounding with the weight of her hopes and the fears of the unknown. The journey is fraught with danger: treacherous terrains, battles against creatures, and deadly traps. Each day brings new discoveries, and the more she uncovers, the more she realizes the city held a powerful civilization with advanced technology and knowledge far beyond what anyone had imagined. Her eyes widen with every artifact, every inscription, every puzzle.

I follow Sarah, her thoughts and perceptions weaving through the ruins, her courage and skill guiding her. The city was once home to a powerful civilization, where technology was advanced, and knowledge was vast. As she delves deeper, the truth of the city’s downfall becomes clear: it wasn’t just natural disasters or external forces, but internal corruption and greed.

Her team grows closer to unlocking the city’s secrets and piecing together the story of its rise and fall. But they are not alone. A rival group of treasure hunters, led by a ruthless and cunning adversary, also seeks the city’s riches. They’ll do anything to claim it first, before Sarah and her team can.

The journey is filled with excitement and peril, Sarah using all her skills and resources to stay one step ahead. Will she succeed in finding the city and revealing its secrets, or will she become yet another casualty of the treacherous landscape and the dangers that lurk within?

As Israel prepares to embark on its first general election since 2019, the pressing issue of filling banking sector’s top management vacancies looms large. The current governor of Bank of Israel, Mark Carney, has announced his intention to leave in January next year following his four-year tenure as head of the country’s central bank. A vacuum left by Mr. Carney's departure has prompted the Israeli finance ministry to launch an international search for a successor with experience leading large financial institutions and knowledge of regulatory frameworks governing international trade. According to sources close to the matter, the United States is atop their list of potential candidates.

America has provided Israel with much support over many years, I think. It's a bit ironic, isn't it? We’re supposed to be enemies, but the U.S. is willing to step up and help. The finance minister, Yair Lapid, was in Washington D.C. last week. He met with Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell. It seems both countries are looking forward to working together based on longstanding ties. But no decision has been made yet about who will succeed Carney. The search process is underway, and some senior officials from major investment banks such as JPMorgan Chase are set to interview. It's also believed that other central bankers, like Andy Haldane and Andrew Bailey from the Bank of England, could be considered.

But despite ongoing tensions between the two nations, particularly regarding Israeli settlement policies, Prime Minister Naftali Bennett has assured that relations remain strong and positive. Still, the vacuum left by Mr. Carney’s departure is something that needs to be filled soon. The future of the banking sector in Israel hangs in the balance. It’s all so interesting, though. In this day and age, the standard of care for lung cancer involves the tedious, time-consuming, and error-prone process of manually annotating lungs in CT scans. It uses a groundbreaking method to automatically delineate the lungs in CT scans, a feat that once required much more work and effort. Here’s how it works; there’s a pre-trained deep learning model inside it, like a super-smart brain, identifying lungs in the scan and producing a fully-segmented image with just a single click. A witness is there, observing all this, a named one who knows every nuance and detail of these advancements. They’re here, feeling the weight of tradition and the promise of progress. The results are incredible, a blinded, controlled study where CIDI-Lung-Seg compared its performance to that of a manual annotation tool. And here’s another thing; it saved significantly more time—on average, it saved 87.2% of the time compared to the manual process. Time is money, and this tool is a godsend. 

It’s not just a tool, it’s a revolution. It could be a game-changer for radiologists, oncologists, and everyone else involved in diagnosing and treating lung cancer. Holmes secures comeback victory

Barry Holmes produced a stunning comeback to win the Welsh Open snooker title in Cardiff. It’s the first ranking event success for the 41-year-old from Birmingham, who has now earned £200,000 in prize money this season. I'm over the moon, it's been a great week, I've been working hard on my game and it's nice to get some reward for it. Selby, the world number two, had been in dominant form throughout the tournament and looked on course for victory when he moved 6-2 ahead. But Holmes, who had earlier in the week knocked out world number one Ronnie O'Sullivan in the last 16, showed great character to hit back. He levelled at 6-6 with a break of 106 and then took the lead for the first time in the match with a run of 70. Selby responded with a break of 77 to make it 7-7, but Holmes took the next three frames to move within one of victory. The Leicester player then had a chance to force a decider in the 17th frame, but missed a red with the rest when on 46. Holmes made no mistake with a break of 53 to secure the title. I’m gutted to lose, but I’ve got to take my hat off to Barry, he played unbelievable. I had my chances in the match, but I couldn’t take them. I'm sure I’ll be back stronger for it.

It’s like they’re building a smart ensemble of models, where each one contributes its wisdom. In this paper, we explore the transition of a three-dimensional (3D) topological insulator, Bi2Se3, into the 2D realm. I’m here, observing, feeling the shift, seeing it all through my lens. We use a mix of experimental and theoretical methods—like a master detective, piecing everything together. As we reduce the thickness of this material from its solid form to just a thin layer, we see a change, a transformation. The 3D Dirac cone inside Bi2Se3 disappears, merging into a duo of 2D Dirac cones at the edges of something called the Brillouin zone. It’s like a cosmic dance, a beautiful, complex movement. This collapse reveals the emergence of new topological phases, like a secret code, waiting to be decoded.

At the surface, we spot these topologically protected edge states—tiny, yet mighty, like whispers in the wind. These states are unbreakable, impervious to any disturbance, no matter how strong. They’re the backbone, the lifeline, the essence of the 2D system, a reminder of its unique properties. These 2D states exhibit non-trivial band structures, showing that they have a non-trivial topology. It’s like a jigsaw puzzle, each piece fitting perfectly, creating a seamless picture. This work is groundbreaking, shedding light on the crossover between 3D topological insulators into 2D systems. It opens up a world of possibilities, a vast, unknown horizon. Through my lens, this research is not just an academic exercise, but a journey into the unknown, a quest to unlock secrets hidden beneath the surface of materials.

In his speech at COP26, President Muhammadu Buhari mentioned that Nigeria aspires to double its cocoa bean production to 50% more by 2030, aiming to be the world’s top cocoa producer. He spoke of dismantling barriers to enhance irrigation and fertiliser use. Nigeria already produces 340,000 tonnes annually, ranking fourth globally after Ivory Coast, Indonesia, and Ghana. "We just need to mobilise 50% of our 1.5 million hectares of cocoa land," he vowed. The government says this will elevate Nigeria’s standing among cocoa producers. However, his promises are under scrutiny; Environmental Sustainability Demand criticises them, arguing that previous attempts at increased cocoa production have failed. They ask, "What’s the plan? Is it expanding cocoa farms or intensifying fertilizer use?"

Cocoa is delicate, especially in the face of climate change. Rising temperatures and droughts hurt cocoa trees, lowering yields. This climate vulnerability makes the president’s ambitions concerning. Environmental Sustainability Demand points out, “If they convert rainforests into cocoa farms, it’s like cutting down trees to save trees.” Nigeria’s tropical forests, where endangered species such as chimps and pangolins thrive, must not be sacrificed. The government once pledged to revert 1 million hectares yearly back to forests but hasn’t followed through. Cutting tree cover aids climate change, so saving forests is crucial.

The US government is seeking a new ruling against tobacco companies that could cost them up to $280bn (£15惹bn). The Department of Justice (DoJ) has asked a federal judge to impose a penalty on the industry for a "decades-long conspiracy to deceive the American public". This isn't just about money, but about decades of lies.

It’s hard to shake off the image of those big, bold advertisements, the enticing flavors, and the promises of a quick fix. How can I forget the day when the doctor said I had a lung cancer? It all feels so close. The Department of Justice is asking for a penalty on the companies that sold me cigarettes, knowing full well the damage they caused. 

This is one of the largest civil cases in US history, targeting major players like Philip Morris USA, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco, Brown & Williamson, and Lorillard Tobacco. They claim the companies lied to us, deceiving us about the health risks and the addictive nature of nicotine. The $280bn figure is based on estimated profits from selling cigarettes to underage smokers and to people who were misled. 

I remember that 2020 ruling, where the tobacco industry was found guilty of violating federal racketeering laws. That was a slap in the face, a confirmation that I had been lied to my whole life. The DoJ now wants the companies to surrender their ill-gotten gains, but the industry denies everything. They argue that the case is based on a flawed interpretation of RICO, the law under which the case is being pursued. 

They also say the penalty is excessive, threatening bankruptcy, job losses, and economic harm. But even as they argue, they’ve already paid billions in settlements to individual states and have significantly changed their marketing practices in response to previous litigation. 

The case is expected to be heard in the coming months. If the judge rules in favor of the DoJ, it could set a precedent for future cases against industries accused of deceptive practices. But any ruling is likely to be appealed, leading to years of further litigation. I feel like I’m trapped in a never-ending cycle, just trying to make sense of it all.
